original_question: Given a Diophantine equation P(x1, ..., xn) = 0, determine whether for every integer k >= 0 there exists an integer solution (x1, ..., xn) such that min(|x1|, ..., |xn|) >= k; if such arbitrarily large solutions do not exist, describe all integer solutions.
target_in_paper: Problem 1 (the "finiteness problem") in the introductory discussion: given a polynomial Diophantine equation, determine whether its set of integer solutions is finite or infinite; if it is finite, find all integer solutions.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly treats the input as a single Diophantine equation of the form P(x1, ..., xn) = 0 and asks for a global property of its integer solution set rather than for just one sample solution. It also correctly anticipates a two-way outcome: one case where no full listing is needed, and another case where all integer solutions should be made explicit.
missing_details: The paper's ambient object is a single polynomial Diophantine equation P(x1, ..., xn) = 0 with P a non-constant polynomial with integer coefficients, i.e. P belongs to Z[x1, ..., xn].
The official decision problem is whether the entire set of integer solutions is finite or infinite, not whether there are solutions with min(|x1|, ..., |xn|) arbitrarily large.
Your condition 'for every integer k >= 0 there exists a solution with min(|x1|, ..., |xn|) >= k' is strictly stronger than infinitude and is not the criterion used in the paper.
In the paper, if the solution set is infinite, one does not have to describe all infinite solutions; proving infinitude already resolves the problem.
In the paper, the requirement to list all integer solutions applies only in the finite case.
The relevant solution set is S = {(x1, ..., xn) in Z^n : P(x1, ..., xn) = 0}.
No restriction on degree, homogeneity, number of variables, or special form of P is part of Problem 1.
The surrounding context matters: the paper introduces Problem 1 as a deliberately relaxed replacement for the harder and less well-posed task of fully describing infinite solution sets.
In the paper's setup, one may assume P is written in reduced form (no two monomials are similar), although this is auxiliary background rather than part of the formal question itself.
The paper studies equations ordered by a size parameter H(P), but that size parameter is not part of the statement of Problem 1 itself.
justification: This is the nearest official formulation to your draft. In the paper's introduction, the author first explains that for larger equations it becomes unclear what it should mean to 'solve' an equation by describing all infinite solution sets, and then explicitly replaces that stronger goal by Problem 1, called the finiteness problem, on page 2. Your draft matches the paper in starting from a general polynomial Diophantine equation and in separating an 'infinite-type' case from a case where all solutions must be listed. However, it departs from the paper at the key point: the paper asks only whether the set of integer solutions is finite or infinite, whereas your 'for every k' condition demands arbitrarily large solutions in all coordinates simultaneously, which is a different and stronger property. The nearby discussion after Problem 1 confirms that, for the paper's intended problem, exhibiting any infinite family of integer solutions is already enough. The later concrete challenge in the paper then specializes this same finiteness problem to the nine equations in Table 1.
